summary: Every week a headline claims a place is getting hotter, wetter or drier. Few people can check it. Real long-term change is hidden in noisy, autocorrelated data; a regional average can hide parts moving in opposite directions; and AI chatbots will happily invent a number. The people who most need trustworthy answers (teachers, students, journalists, farmers and local officials) usually have no data scientist and often don't read English. MEIKA-X puts every trend on trial. Ask a question about any place on Earth and eight AI-assisted agents pull 45 years of NASA data, test whether the change is statistically real, and let a Skeptic try to break it before giving an honest grade from A to D. Every number links to its NASA source, and the verdict is explained in plain language, in English and the local language of the place.
details:
The problem. NASA's Earth data is free and global, but turning it into a trustworthy answer to "is this place really changing?" takes skills most people don't have. Plotting a line is easy; knowing whether it is real is not. Monthly climate data is autocorrelated, so simple tests overstate significance. Regional averages hide opposite trends. The start year changes the story. And general-purpose AI produces confident numbers that come from no dataset. The result is a trust gap: some people believe every alarming headline, others dismiss real change as noise.

What MEIKA-X does. It acts as a court for trends. You type a question in plain words, such as "Are summers in Spain and Portugal getting hotter?", with no sign-up. A Chief Detective agent turns it into a precise test (which NASA variable, which region, which years). Specialist agents then investigate in a 3D lab you can watch:

  • a Statistician measures the trend and its uncertainty;
  • a Satellite Witness checks fresh MODIS imagery and NASA EONET natural events;
  • a Driver Analyst tests possible causes and their time lags;
  • a Skeptic runs seven tests that try to break the result;
  • a Forecaster estimates near-term hazard odds against the old climate;
  • Exposure counts events and active fires in the region;
  • a Narrator explains the verdict in plain language.

You get an evidence grade (A to D), the trend per decade with its 95% interval, a map of where the change happens, satellite images, and an evidence ledger where every number links to the exact NASA query it came from. A chat assistant answers follow-up questions, and active monitoring watches chosen regions daily and sends alerts to Telegram.

How it works, and why it can be trusted. Every statistic comes from deterministic, unit-tested code cross-checked against scipy and pymannkendall:

  • a least-squares trend with an autocorrelation-adjusted t-test, a Mann-Kendall test with the Hamed-Rao correction, and Sen's slope;
  • a block-bootstrap interval and Pettitt change-point detection;
  • per-cell trends with false-discovery-rate control, which flags "opposite stories" where one part of a region warms while another cools.

AI is used only to plan, explain and describe, and an automated check rejects any AI-written number that is not in the ledger. When the evidence is weak, MEIKA-X says "no case yet" and estimates how many more years of data would be needed.

Example. Daily maximum temperature over the Iberian Peninsula rose by +0.354 °C per decade from 1981 to 2025 (95% interval 0.235 to 0.472). It earned grade B: significant in both tests and passing every Skeptic check. Grade A is reserved for confirmation from an independent sensor dataset. On 15 November 2026 the monitor caught a real heat anomaly in the Central Amazon (36.2 °C against a 1991–2020 normal of 31.9 °C) and sent the alert to Telegram automatically.

Benefits and intended impact.

  • Anyone can test a climate claim about their own place in minutes and get evidence they can check and cite.
  • Teachers get a live lesson in how scientists separate signal from noise.
  • Journalists get graded, sourced numbers instead of guesses.
  • Communities get early, data-backed alerts.

The aim is to close the trust gap: fewer people fooled by noise, fewer people dismissing real change.

How it is creative. The courtroom metaphor makes scientific rigour visible. Agents walk to the terminal of the NASA service they are calling, a Skeptic cross-examines every finding, and the verdict comes with an evidence grade rather than a yes or no. Users watch how a result was reached, not just the result.

Factors we considered.

  • Accessibility: no login, plain language, briefs in the local language (Spanish, Portuguese, French, Swahili, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, Vietnamese, Russian and more), and a layout that works on phones.
  • Cost: free NASA open data, free hosting tiers, and an app that still works fully, with simpler wording, if no AI model is available.
  • Honesty: uncertainty is always shown, correlations are labelled as associations, and hazard odds are clearly not weather forecasts.
  • Reproducibility: fixed random seeds, so the same case gives the same ledger.
  • Privacy: no accounts, so no personal data is stored.
  • Tools. TypeScript, Next.js 16, React and Three.js; Supabase (Postgres and Storage); Vercel hosting and cron; the Telegram Bot API. For AI, Claude Opus 5.5 is our primary model. Because our hackathon AI credits are limited, the public demo falls back to Groq's free tier (GPT-OSS 120B), with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on Hugging Face as a further backup.
